sentences.text: Dapedium was covered in thick ganoid scales, a type of tough, enamel-like armor found in ancient fish.
Its robust lower jaw held slender, single-cusped or two-cusped marginal teeth, while smaller interior teeth on the skull formed dense batteries.
The only known specimen of Dapedium from eastern Europe is a complete fossil from the Toarcian of Hungary.
Fossil evidence suggests the fish engaged in scavenging, as one individual was found trapped inside the body cavity of an ammonite.
William Elford Leach named the genus in 1822, describing the type species D. politum from Early Jurassic remains in Lyme Regis, Dorset, England.
While relatively rare during the Triassic, the fish experienced a large burst in diversification following the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event.
Researchers suggest Dapedium survived this extinction because it was a heavily-scaled generalist, unlike most Triassic dapediids which had specialized feeding or less armor.
It is thought to have been a durophagous predator that used slender marginal teeth to grasp prey and smaller interior teeth to crush hard-shelled organisms.
Adaptations in Dapedium may have helped it survive the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event, though its abundance declined dramatically around that time and it went extinct shortly after.
Dapedius is a synonym for the genus Dapedium, which belongs to the extinct order Semionotiformes and the family Dapediidae.
Dapedium lived from the Late Triassic to the Middle Jurassic, spanning the late Norian to early Aalenian stages.
It inhabited the western Tethys Ocean surrounding Europe, with fossils found in Italy, the UK, France, Germany, and Hungary.
The monophyly of the genus Dapedium is debated, with some studies suggesting it is probably paraphyletic.
